solution: The ball model, pinned down by the samples: from cell (i,j) a '\\' wall rolls it down-right - it leaves by the right edge when j = N, and it is STUCK when cell (i,j+1) is '/' because the two diagonals meet in a V at their shared bottom corner; otherwise it enters (i+1,j+1) and exits the bottom at column j+1 when i = M. '/' is the mirror image. The V rule is what the last sample tests: flipping (4,4), a cell off the path, turns an exit into -1. For the queries, sqrt-decompose the ROWS. When M <= N a drop is simulated directly in O(M) = O(sqrt(MN)) steps; otherwise N < sqrt(MN) and rows are cut into blocks of B = sqrt(M/N) rows, each storing entry column -> exit column or dead, built in O(B*N). A drop walks M/B blocks and a flip rebuilds one block, both O(sqrt(M*N)). Total O(MN + Q sqrt(MN)) time, O(MN) space.
statement_summary: A board of M rows and N columns holds one diagonal wall per cell, slanting either way. A ball dropped at the top of a column slides along the walls and either leaves sideways, jams between two walls, or reaches the bottom. Queries flip one wall or drop a ball, reporting its bottom exit column or minus one. Cell count and query count are each at most 100000.
notes: Confidence is 0.85 only because the wall physics is inferred rather than stated: the rule '\ then / to its right = stuck' is the unique model I found that reproduces all five sample answers, in particular the final -1 caused by flipping (4,4), which lies off the ball's path. Ambiguous peaks ('/' left of '\' below the corner) are resolved by keeping the ball's momentum; no sample distinguishes that case. verify_droppingball.py checks the sample and matches the block structure against naive step-by-step simulation on 300 random boards plus tall/wide shapes. A segment tree over rows storing column->exit maps also works but its update is O(N log M), worse than sqrt in the tall regime.
